assumptions: EXECUTE AS OWNER was chosen over CALLER to match Teradata macro semantics, where referenced objects are accessed with the immediate owner's rights. Switch to EXECUTE AS CALLER if the target security model requires caller rights.
CURRENT_DATE() is evaluated in the Snowflake session TIMEZONE, while Teradata used the session/system time zone. Align TIMEZONE if day boundaries matter.
SALES.DAILY_BALANCE.AMOUNT and SALES."ACCOUNT".BALANCE are assumed to have the same DECIMAL precision and scale in the converted DDL, as in the source. Teradata bare DECIMAL is DECIMAL(5,0).
Called in autocommit mode (not inside an open explicit transaction), so the INSERT commits or rolls back as a single statement, like a single-statement Teradata macro request.

Callers must change EXEC sales.refresh_daily[(...)] to CALL SALES.REFRESH_DAILY([...]); Teradata's positional empty-argument syntax (e.g. EXEC m(,)) has no equivalent. Omit the argument to get the default.
Returning SQLROWCOUNT stands in for Teradata ACTIVITY_COUNT. The macro itself returned no result set.
explanations: Teradata macro converted to a Snowflake Scripting procedure (LANGUAGE SQL, EXECUTE AS OWNER) with a defaulted DATE argument.
The single INSERT ... SELECT is unchanged apart from object names and the :P_DAY bind reference; no new casts are needed because P_DAY is DATE and the other columns copy across unchanged.
The EXCEPTION WHEN OTHER THEN RAISE handler keeps Teradata's fail-and-roll-back behaviour visible to the caller.

Object names follow the naming map (SALES.* unquoted, SALES."ACCOUNT" quoted because ACCOUNT is a Snowflake reserved word); the database is not named in the naming map so names are schema-qualified and resolve against the current database.

-- Converted: Teradata CREATE MACRO sales.refresh_daily(p_day DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE) rewritten as Snowflake Scripting stored procedure SALES.REFRESH_DAILY with an optional DATE argument P_DAY DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE(); EXECUTE AS OWNER declared; returns the inserted row count.
-- Reason: Snowflake has no macros; a SQL stored procedure is the closest equivalent. Teradata macros access referenced objects with the privileges of the macro's immediate owner, so EXECUTE AS OWNER keeps that privilege model. The DEFAULT is only applied when the argument is omitted, so an explicit NULL is still inserted as NULL, as in Teradata. Invoke with CALL SALES.REFRESH_DAILY(); or CALL SALES.REFRESH_DAILY(TO_DATE('2025-01-31', 'YYYY-MM-DD')); instead of EXEC.
CREATE PROCEDURE SALES.REFRESH_DAILY(P_DAY DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE())
RETURNS NUMBER(38,0)
LANGUAGE SQL
EXECUTE AS OWNER
AS
$$
BEGIN
  -- Converted: INSERT ... SELECT p_day, account_id, balance FROM sales.account converted to Snowflake with fully qualified target names, the bind variable :P_DAY and the reserved-word table SALES."ACCOUNT".
  -- Reason: Snowflake Scripting references procedure arguments inside SQL with a colon prefix; ACCOUNT is reserved in Snowflake and is mapped to SALES."ACCOUNT". P_DAY is already DATE and BALANCE_DATE is DATE, so no implicit conversion takes place.
  INSERT INTO SALES.DAILY_BALANCE (BALANCE_DATE, ACCOUNT_ID, AMOUNT)
  SELECT :P_DAY, ACCOUNT_ID, BALANCE
  FROM SALES."ACCOUNT";
  RETURN SQLROWCOUNT;
EXCEPTION
  -- Converted: Added an EXCEPTION handler that re-raises the original error.
  -- Reason: A Teradata macro aborts and rolls back its request when a statement fails. The single INSERT runs as one autocommit statement, so it rolls back on its own, and re-raising passes the original error to the caller without swallowing it.
  WHEN OTHER THEN
    RAISE;
END;
$$;

FROM SALES.CUSTOMER AS c
